stem.text: An oligopolist with a kinked demand curve decides to raise its price.

options.text: it has a large increase in costs
it is starting a predatory pricing strategy
it is trying to price discriminate
it wants to start a price war

explanation.text: The kinked demand curve model explains why oligopolists keep prices stable: above the current price, demand is highly elastic (rivals won't follow a price rise, so the firm loses a lot of market share), while below it, demand is inelastic (rivals match any price cut, so little is gained). This makes the firm reluctant to change price at all — unless a cost increase is so large that it can no longer be absorbed within the flat (discontinuous) range of the marginal cost curve at the kink, forcing a price rise despite the risk of losing customers.

optionAnalysis.text: A sufficiently large cost increase can push MC above the discontinuous range at the kink, forcing even a price-stable kinked-demand firm to raise price — this is the standard reason prices do change under this model.
Predatory pricing means setting price very low (often below cost) to drive out rivals, the opposite of raising price.
Price discrimination means charging different prices to different consumer groups for the same good, not a reason to raise the single posted price.
A price war is started by cutting price aggressively to undercut rivals, not by raising price.

reasoningChain: Recall that the kinked demand curve model predicts price rigidity: firms avoid changing price because any price change (up or down) leaves them worse off relative to rivals matching or not matching.
Identify the one circumstance that still forces a price change despite this rigidity: a cost shock large enough to move MC outside the vertical/discontinuous portion of the MC curve at the kink.

Match this to option A; the other three options describe aggressive pricing strategies (predatory, price war) or a different pricing policy (discrimination), none of which explain a reluctant price rise under kinked demand.

inferredMistakes.text: Treating a price rise as evidence of some aggressive competitive strategy (predatory pricing, a price war) rather than recognising that the kinked demand model predicts firms avoid raising price unless forced to by costs.

bullets: Options B, C and D were equally popular incorrect answers.
This suggests that many candidates did not understand that a key characteristic of an oligopolistic market is the lack of price competition which negates each of these three options.
